title: Why a short hurts
description: A short is an easy extra path. Current and heat soar. That is not a brighter circuit you get to keep.

blocks.md:
## Easy path, ugly ending

A short is not “more electricity, so better.” It is a low-resistance shortcut around the part that was doing the work. Current prefers the easy wire. The lamp is skipped. The easy wire and the battery take a huge I. Power P = V × I becomes heat in a thin place. That is how insulation smells and fuses exist.

This bites when a demo looks dramatic — a fat spark, a bright flash — and someone files it under “more power.” The useful lamp was the first casualty.

![A short skips the lamp](assets/short-path.svg)

```text
battery ──SHORT── battery     (huge I, heat)
        ╲ lamp ╱              (often dark)
```

A common mistake is wiring a bypass “to help the lamp.” The questions ask you to name the danger and the reason.

blocks.promptMd: Someone adds a thick wire from one battery end to the other, skipping the lamp. What is that, and why is it bad?

choices.md: A power boost for a better lamp

reasons.md: Huge current becomes heat on the easy path.
More metal always means a brighter useful lamp.

blocks.explainMd: It is a short. The easy path takes the current. Heat follows. The lamp is not helped.

blocks.promptMd: Which picture is the dangerous shortcut?
blocks.explainMd: The red bypass is the short. Open is dark and usually safe. Closed is the job.

blocks.promptMd: A short is how you give a lamp extra useful power.
blocks.explainMd: A short skips the lamp and overheats the easy wire.
